title: Siang Dam Is India's Buffer Against China's Brahmaputra Mega-Dam
excerpt: China's 60,000 MW Medog dam is already under construction upstream. India's 11,200 MW Siang project is New Delhi's storage answer — and the Adi villages in its path are asking who pays for that security.
body:
• China began building a 60,000 MW mega-dam at Medog in Tibet in July 2025 on the Yarlung Tsangpo, the river that enters India as the Siang and later forms the Brahmaputra.
  • India's proposed 11,200 MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project is designed as a storage buffer: about 9.2 billion cubic metres of live storage, compared with an estimated 5.5 BCM for the Medog project.
  • Adi community groups in Arunachal Pradesh oppose the project, estimating 27 villages could be submerged; the project is still only at the pre-feasibility survey stage, before social and environmental assessments.
  • For diaspora families with roots in Assam and Arunachal, the outcome will shape flood risk and water security across the Brahmaputra basin for decades.

India's Siang Upper Multipurpose Project is not primarily a power project. It is a storage project, proposed because China is building the world's largest hydropower dam upstream on the same river — and because whoever controls storage on this river can soften, or sharpen, what happens downstream.

The river begins in Tibet as the Yarlung Tsangpo. It flows east, turns sharply south at the Great Bend, enters Arunachal Pradesh as the Siang or Dihang, runs about 294 km through the state, and then joins the Dibang and Lohit in Assam to form the Brahmaputra, according to Jagran's explainer on the project.

What China Is Building at Medog

In July 2025, China launched construction of a massive hydropower project in Medog county in Tibet, near the Great Bend. The project is expected to generate around 60,000 MW — nearly three times the capacity of the Three Gorges Dam — with an estimated investment of 1.2 trillion yuan. Its scale comes from the steep drop of the river at the bend, not from a large reservoir.

That distinction matters. Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Pema Khandu has pointed out that Medog's estimated live storage is about 5.5 billion cubic metres, despite its far larger generation capacity. For India and Bangladesh, the concern is not only how much electricity China generates, but whether an upstream operator could change the timing and volume of releases — holding water back in a dry season or discharging it suddenly — with consequences for flood management and water security downstream.

Why India Wants Storage on the Siang

The Siang Upper project, implemented by NHPC and spread across Upper Siang, Siang and East Siang districts, is designed for 11,200 MW of generation but about 9.2 BCM of live storage — more storage than Medog, on a smaller power plant. The Centre's logic is that a large downstream reservoir could absorb sudden upstream releases, sustain flows through the year and protect the Siang-Brahmaputra basin, as Illustrated Daily News reported. Khandu has described China's project in stark terms and argued the Indian dam would moderate floods if China releases water.

The idea is not new. The Siang project was first proposed in 1983 and designated a national project in 2008. It gained fresh momentum after the Union Cabinet decided in September this year to conduct a pre-feasibility survey — the step now under way, and the step protesters are trying to stop.

Why Arunachal Locals Are Opposing It

For the Adi community living along the Siang, the strategic argument is weighed against land they stand to lose. The Siang Indigenous Farmers Forum estimates the reservoir would submerge 27 villages and displace more than 1.5 lakh residents, threatening paddy fields and traditional livelihoods. Those are the forum's own figures, and the exact submergence area has not been publicly settled. Groups including Adi Baane Kebang-United, the SUMP-Affected Youth Association and the Adi Galo Welfare Society also cite heritage sites at risk, including Kekar Moying, associated with the Anglo-Abor battle, and object to surveys conducted without the consent of affected communities.

That opposition turned violent in East Siang in October, when protesters torched an NHPC office and a police station and the Centre airlifted about 250 Rapid Action Force personnel to Pasighat — events The Videshi covered separately. The explainer question behind the violence is whether a national-security project can proceed before the people in its path have been heard.

What Happens Next

A pre-feasibility report is not a construction clearance. Khandu has said that if the survey finds the project viable, it must still undergo a Social Impact Assessment, an Environmental Impact Assessment and a Detailed Project Report. Several villages have signed agreements to allow initial survey work, and the state government says it will consult affected communities before moving forward. Whether that consultation persuades Adi landowners — and whether Beijing offers any transparency on Medog's operations — will decide if India's buffer gets built at all.
